newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Cuban-born U.S. politicians slam EU on Helms-Burton.
newsitem.headline: Cuban-born U.S. politicians slam EU on Helms-Burton.

text.p: Two Cuban-born members of the United States Congress warned on Friday that the European Union "may have bitten off more than it can chew" in challenging Washington's Helms-Burton laws at the World Trade Organisation.

Lincoln Diaz-Balart and Ileana Ros-Lehtinen told a news conference that the U.S. would not tolerate any world body ordering it to lift a visa ban on individuals deemed to be dealing in property stolen by Cuba's government from Americans.
"If you think this is going to get Helms-Burton changed, then you are barking up the wrong tree," said Diaz-Balart, a Republican congressman from Miami, Florida.
Relations between the EU and Washington have been hit by differences over the Helms-Burton Act -- an amalgamation of decades of U.S. anti-Cuba policy -- and the matter is now before the WTO.

But Ros-Lehtinen, also a republican from Miami, warned: "Congress voted for the Helms-Burton law to be passed by a majority of over 400. Congress voted to join the WTO by less than 150 ... work it out".

Among other things, the Act allows naturalised Americans to sue in U.S. courts foreigners deemed to have benefited from property confiscated by the Cuban government since the Communist revolution of 1959.

Although this part has twice been suspended by President Bill Clinton, another section allows Washington to prohibit entry to the U.S. to executives, shareholders and representives of companies investing in confiscated property.
"No country that I know of would allow the WTO to tell them who can and cannot pass through their borders," said Diaz-Balart.
"If we go back to Congress with this message there would be uproar in both houses. I don't think the Europeans have thought through what it means to get involved in the immigration issue."

Diaz-Balart said the EU's WTO action was "misguided, over-zealous, and wholly without merit" and stressed that Washington's motives for passing the laws was entirely justified on national security grounds.
The act became law last March when four American citizens were killed when the light aircraft in which they were flying in international airspace near Cuba were shot down by Cuban jet fighters.
The two members of Congress said they would be sponsoring a campaign from next week to inform Americans of the WTO action and the threat it posed to U.S. sovereignty.
"This action is a depth-charge for the WTO," said Ros-Lehtinen.
Washington on Thursday challenged the fitness of the WTO to adjudicate a dispute over U.S. sanctions on Cuba and said it would not cooperate with the investigative panel.
Undersecretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstat said Washington would try to settle its differences with the EU directly but would not cooperate with the WTO panel.
"The WTO is not an appropriate forum for resolving differences over what is essentially a disagreement over foreign policy," he said.
U.S. officials say the Cuba sanctions policy is legal under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, the set of open trading rules that underpins the WTO.

Washington cites GATT's Article XXI on "Security Exceptions," which says nothing in the accord should prevent a signatory "from taking any action which it considers necessary for the protection of its essential security interests."
EU members and other U.S. trading partners challenge this U.S. interpretation and say Washington's use of the security exception in this case is not legitimate.
